questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The universal gravitational constant is G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Given 1 N = 10⁵ dyne, its value in CGS units (dyne cm² g⁻²) is:

solution.concept: Conversion of a derived unit between systems
solution.explanation: Replace each SI unit by its CGS equivalent: 1 N = 10⁵ dyne, 1 m² = 10⁴ cm² and 1 kg⁻² = (10³ g)⁻² = 10⁻⁶ g⁻².
solution.why_others_wrong: 10⁻¹⁰ converts m² as if 1 m² = 10² cm². 10⁻¹³ leaves the newton unconverted. 10⁴ multiplies by 10⁶ for kg⁻² instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', the international system of units

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following physical quantities has the dimensional formula [M L⁰ T⁻³]?

options.text: Intensity of a wave (power transmitted per unit area)

solution.concept: Dimensional formula of a derived quantity
solution.explanation: Power is energy per unit time, [M L² T⁻³]. Dividing by an area [L²] removes the length dimension, leaving [M T⁻³].
steps: Intensity = power/area = [M L² T⁻³]/[L²] = [M L⁰ T⁻³]
solution.why_others_wrong: Surface tension (force per length) is [M T⁻²]; power is [M L² T⁻³]; pressure is [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional formulae
solution.final_answer: Option C: Intensity of a wave (power transmitted per unit area)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a new system of units, the unit of force is 10 N, the unit of energy is 100 J and the unit of velocity is 5 m s⁻¹. The unit of time in this system is equal to:

solution.concept: Building units of a new system from chosen derived units
solution.explanation: Energy = force × length, so the unit of length is (100 J)/(10 N). Time = length/velocity then gives the unit of time.
steps: Unit of length = 100 J / 10 N = 10 m
Unit of time = 10 m / (5 m s⁻¹) = 2 s
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 s inverts the last step (velocity/length). 4 s is the numerical value of the unit of mass (E/v² = 4 kg), not of time. 50 s multiplies the length by the velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensions and dimensional analysis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (source of error in a measurement) with List-II (type of error, as classified in NCERT).

List-I:
A. The zero mark of the vernier scale does not coincide with the zero of the main scale when the jaws of a vernier calliper are closed
B. An observer, out of habit, always reads a needle with the head slightly to one side, introducing parallax
C. Body temperature is measured by placing a thermometer under the armpit, which always gives a value lower than the actual body temperature
D. Unpredictable fluctuations in the readings caused by unpredictable changes in the supply voltage

List-II:
I. Random error
II. Instrumental error
III. Personal error
IV. Error due to imperfection in experimental technique or procedure

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Systematic and random errors
solution.explanation: NCERT divides systematic errors into instrumental errors (imperfect design or calibration, such as a zero error), errors from imperfect experimental technique or procedure (the armpit thermometer always reads low) and personal errors (an observer's bias or habit, such as a parallax habit). Errors that occur irregularly and are random in size and sign, like those from supply-voltage fluctuations, are random errors.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes confuse the armpit thermometer (a faulty procedure) with an instrument fault or a personal habit, or call a systematic error random.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', errors in measurement (systematic and random errors)
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the relation y = a sin(bt − cx), where y and x are distances and t is time, the ratio b/c has the dimensions of speed.
Reason (R): The argument of a trigonometric function must be dimensionless, so bt and cx must each be dimensionless.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Dimensionless arguments of functions
solution.explanation: An angle is a pure number, so bt and cx must each be dimensionless. That forces [b] = [T⁻¹] and [c] = [L⁻¹], and b/c = [L T⁻¹], the dimensions of speed. The reason is exactly what fixes the dimensions in A.
steps: [b/c] = L T⁻¹ (speed) → A true, R explains
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R is the very rule used to find [b] and [c], so options B, C and D fail.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional analysis and its applications
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The specific heat capacity of a liquid is found from c = Q/(mΔθ), where the heat Q supplied by a calibrated heater may be taken as exact. The mass of the liquid is (200 ± 2) g, and its initial and final temperatures are (20.0 ± 0.5) °C and (45.0 ± 0.5) °C. The maximum percentage error in c is:

solution.concept: Error of a difference combined with a quotient
solution.explanation: The rise in temperature is a difference, so its absolute errors add. Its relative error then adds to the relative error of the mass, because c is a quotient.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3% takes the error of Δθ as 0.5 °C instead of 1.0 °C. 1% subtracts the two temperature errors (0.5 − 0.5) and keeps only the mass error. About 4.6% uses the relative errors of the two temperature readings instead of the error of their difference.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A quantity having the dimensions of time is to be formed from Planck's constant h [M L² T⁻¹], the universal gravitational constant G [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²] and the speed of light c [L T⁻¹], without any other constant. Ignoring dimensionless factors, this quantity is:

solution.concept: Constructing a quantity by equating dimensions
solution.explanation: Write t = h^a G^b c^d and equate the powers of M, L and T on both sides. The three equations fix a, b and d uniquely.
solution.why_others_wrong: √(hc/G) has the dimensions of mass, √(hG/c³) of length and √(hc⁵/G) of energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', deducing relations by the method of dimensions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A stone is thrown vertically upward with a speed of 15 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its velocity 2 s after the throw is:

options.text: zero, because the stone is at its highest point

solution.concept: Velocity under uniform acceleration with sign convention
solution.explanation: Take upward as positive. The acceleration is −g throughout, so v = u − gt. A negative result means the stone has passed its highest point (at 1.5 s) and is falling.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Upward' drops the sign of the answer. 35 m/s adds gt to u as if g pointed upward. The highest point is reached at u/g = 1.5 s, not at 2 s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body starts from rest and moves along a straight line with uniform acceleration. The distances it covers in successive equal intervals of time (the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th interval) are in the ratio:

solution.concept: Galileo's law of odd numbers
solution.explanation: From rest, the distance covered up to the end of the nth interval τ is ½a(nτ)², proportional to n². The distance in the nth interval alone is proportional to n² − (n − 1)² = 2n − 1, the odd numbers.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 are the total distances from the start, not the distances in each interval. 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 would be the velocities at the ends of the intervals. 1 : √2 : √3 : 2 are the times to cover equal distances from rest, measured from the start.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations (Galileo's law of odd numbers)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For the vectors A = 2î + 3ĵ and B = î + ĵ, the magnitude of A + B is:

solution.concept: Adding vectors by components
solution.explanation: Add the x-components and the y-components separately, then find the magnitude of the resultant.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 adds the components 3 + 4 without squaring. √5 is the magnitude of A − B. √13 + √2 adds the magnitudes, which is valid only for parallel vectors.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', vector addition: analytical method

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The angular speed of the minute hand of a clock that is keeping correct time is:

solution.concept: Angular speed from the period
solution.explanation: The minute hand turns through 2π rad in one hour (3600 s) at a steady rate, so ω = 2π/T.
solution.why_others_wrong: π/30 rad/s is the angular speed of the seconds hand (T = 60 s). π/3600 rad/s forgets the factor 2 in 2π. π/21600 rad/s is the hour hand (T = 12 h).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', uniform circular motion (angular speed)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car travels the first half of the distance between two towns at a constant speed of 40 km/h and the second half at a constant speed of 60 km/h, along a straight road. Its average speed for the whole journey is:

solution.concept: Average speed as total distance over total time
solution.explanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. With equal distances, the slower half takes longer, so the average is weighted towards the lower speed: it is the harmonic mean 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂).
steps: Let each half be d: total time = d/40 + d/60 = d/24
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 km/h is the arithmetic mean, true only for equal time intervals. 24 km/h forgets that the total distance is 2d. 52 km/h weights the average towards the faster speed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', average velocity and average speed

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground with a speed of 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its height above the ground when it has moved a horizontal distance of 10√3 m is:

solution.concept: Independence of horizontal and vertical motion
solution.explanation: The horizontal velocity u cos θ is constant, so the horizontal distance fixes the time. That time then gives the height from the vertical motion, which has acceleration −g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 m ignores the fall due to gravity (u_y t only). 15 m adds ½gt² instead of subtracting it. 2.5 m uses ½ × ½gt² for the drop and the wrong sign.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Ship A sails due east at 10 m/s and ship B sails due north at 10 m/s, both with constant velocities. The velocity of ship B relative to ship A is:

solution.concept: Relative velocity in two dimensions
solution.explanation: v_BA = v_B − v_A. Subtracting an eastward velocity is the same as adding a westward one, so B appears to A to move north and west at once.
solution.why_others_wrong: North-east adds v_A instead of subtracting it. 20 m/s towards north adds the magnitudes as if the velocities were parallel. South-east is the velocity of A relative to B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', relative velocity in two dimensions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The velocity–time graph of a particle moving along a straight line is a single straight line going from +10 m/s at t = 0 to −10 m/s at t = 4 s. For the interval t = 0 to t = 4 s, its displacement and the distance it travels are respectively:

solution.concept: Displacement and distance from a velocity–time graph
solution.explanation: The area between the v–t graph and the time axis gives displacement, with area below the axis counted negative. Distance adds the magnitudes of the areas. The line crosses the axis at t = 2 s.
steps: Area from 0 to 2 s = ½ × 2 × 10 = +10 m
Area from 2 s to 4 s = −10 m
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 m for displacement ignores the sign of the area below the axis. 0 for distance forgets that the particle actually moves. 40 m doubles the area of each triangle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', velocity–time graph and displacement

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If two vectors of equal magnitude P have a resultant of magnitude P, the angle between them is 120°.
Statement II: If two vectors of equal magnitude P are inclined at 60° to each other, the magnitude of their difference is P√3.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Resultant and difference of two equal vectors
solution.explanation: For two vectors of magnitude P at angle θ, |A + B|² = 2P²(1 + cos θ) and |A − B|² = 2P²(1 − cos θ), that is |A + B| = 2P cos(θ/2) and |A − B| = 2P sin(θ/2).
steps: Statement I: P² = 2P²(1 + cos θ) → cos θ = −½ → θ = 120° (true)
Statement II: |A − B| = 2P sin 30° = P, not P√3 (false; P√3 is |A + B| at 60°)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II gives the magnitude of the sum, not the difference, so options A, B and D fail.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', addition and subtraction of vectors
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle starts from rest at the origin and moves along the positive x-axis so that its velocity at position x is v = 4√x, with v in m/s and x in metres. The distance it covers in the first 2 s is:

solution.concept: Acceleration from velocity as a function of position
solution.explanation: With v given as a function of x, a = v(dv/dx). For v = β√x this is a constant, β²/2, so the particle moves with uniform acceleration from rest.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 m uses a = 4 m/s² (β instead of β²/2). 32 m forgets the factor ½ in ½at². 64 m takes x = (vt)² with v = 4 m/s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', instantaneous velocity and acceleration

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle is projected from level ground with a speed of 20 m/s at 60° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the radius of curvature of its path at the highest point is:

solution.concept: Projectile at its highest point as instantaneous circular motion
solution.explanation: At the top the velocity is horizontal (u cos θ) and the acceleration g is vertical, i.e. perpendicular to the velocity. So g acts as the centripetal acceleration: g = v²/r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 m uses the full launch speed (u²/g). 30 m uses the vertical component of the launch velocity. 15 m is the maximum height, not the radius of curvature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion and centripetal acceleration

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The position of a particle moving along the x-axis is x = 5 + 4t − t², with x in metres and t in seconds. Consider its motion from t = 0 to t = 4 s. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The particle reverses its direction of motion at t = 2 s.
(b) Its displacement over the interval t = 0 to t = 4 s is zero.
(c) The distance it travels over the interval t = 0 to t = 4 s is 4 m.
(d) Its acceleration is zero at t = 2 s.
(e) Its speed at t = 4 s is 4 m/s.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Velocity, acceleration, distance and displacement from x(t)
solution.explanation: v = dx/dt = 4 − 2t and a = −2 m/s² (constant). The particle stops and turns back where v = 0. Distance must be added in pieces on either side of the turning point.
steps: (a) v = 0 at t = 2 s and changes sign → true
(b) x(0) = 5 m, x(4) = 5 m → displacement 0 → true
(c) x(2) = 9 m: distance = 4 + 4 = 8 m, not 4 m → false
(d) a = −2 m/s² at all times → false (v = 0 does not mean a = 0)
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) halve the distance; options with (d) confuse momentary rest with zero acceleration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', instantaneous velocity and acceleration

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A man standing on a platform that moves vertically upward with a constant velocity throws a ball vertically upward. Neglecting air resistance, the time after which the ball returns to his hand is the same as it would be if the platform were at rest.
Statement II: An observer on the ground finds the ball momentarily at rest at the instant when it is at its greatest height above the man.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Relative motion in a frame moving with constant velocity
solution.explanation: Relative to the platform, the ball starts with the throw speed u and has acceleration g downward (the platform does not accelerate), so it returns after 2u/g, just as on a fixed platform. At its greatest height above the man, the ball's velocity relative to him is zero, so relative to the ground it moves upward with the platform's velocity, not zero.
steps: Relative acceleration = g − 0 = g; relative initial velocity = u → return time 2u/g (Statement I true)
Greatest height above the man: v_ball − v_platform = 0 → v_ball = v_platform ≠ 0 (Statement II false)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II mixes the man's frame with the ground frame; in the ground frame the ball is at rest only later, when it reaches its greatest height above the ground.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', relative velocity
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The linear momentum of a body moving along a straight line varies with time as p = 2t² + 3t, where p is in kg m/s and t in seconds. The net force acting on the body at t = 2 s is:

solution.concept: Newton's second law as rate of change of momentum
solution.explanation: The net force equals the instantaneous rate of change of linear momentum, F = dp/dt.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 N is the momentum (in kg m/s) at t = 2 s, not its rate of change. 8 N drops the 3t term's derivative. 7 N is the average p/t, which is not the instantaneous force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: At a certain instant, the net force acting on a moving body is directed due north. Which of the following must be true at that instant?

options.text: The velocity of the body is directed due north
The body is moving due north with increasing speed
The velocity and the acceleration of the body are both directed due north
The acceleration of the body is directed due north, but its velocity may be in any direction

solution.concept: Force fixes acceleration, not velocity
solution.explanation: By the second law, F = ma, so the acceleration is always along the net force. The velocity at an instant depends on the past motion: a body thrown upward has a downward force on it while it still moves up, and a body in circular motion has a force perpendicular to its velocity.
steps: a is parallel to F_net → a is due north
Velocity is not fixed by the force at that instant
solution.why_others_wrong: All the other options tie the velocity to the force, which is not required (e.g. a body moving south while being slowed down by a northward force).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion
solution.final_answer: Option D: The acceleration of the body is directed due north, but its velocity may be in any direction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wooden box rests on the horizontal floor of a truck. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor is 0.4. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum acceleration with which the truck can start moving along a level road without the box slipping on its floor is:

solution.concept: Static friction as the force that accelerates a body
solution.explanation: The only horizontal force on the box is the static friction from the floor, so it must supply ma. The largest value it can take is μₛmg, which limits the acceleration to μₛg, whatever the mass of the box.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.4 m/s² forgets to multiply by g. 40 m/s² multiplies by 100 instead of g. 25 m/s² divides g by μₛ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction (static friction)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle is in equilibrium under the action of three coplanar concurrent forces. Which of the following must be true?

options.text: The three forces must be equal in magnitude
The three forces can be represented in magnitude and direction by the three sides of a triangle taken in the same order
The three forces must be mutually perpendicular
One of the forces must be greater than the sum of the other two

solution.concept: Equilibrium under three concurrent forces
solution.explanation: For equilibrium the vector sum of the forces must be zero: F₁ + F₂ + F₃ = 0. Placing the forces head to tail then closes the figure, so they form the sides of a triangle taken in order.
steps: Head-to-tail placement returns to the start → closed triangle
solution.why_others_wrong: The forces need not be equal or perpendicular (three mutually perpendicular forces cannot even be coplanar and sum to zero). If one force exceeded the sum of the others, they could never cancel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle
solution.final_answer: Option B: The three forces can be represented in magnitude and direction by the three sides of a triangle taken in the same order

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball of mass 0.2 kg is dropped from rest from a height of 5 m onto a hard horizontal floor and rebounds vertically to a height of 1.25 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the magnitude of the impulse exerted by the floor on the ball is:

solution.concept: Impulse as change in momentum, with direction
solution.explanation: The impulse equals the change in momentum. The ball reaches the floor moving down and leaves it moving up, so the change in velocity is the sum of the two speeds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 N s subtracts the speeds, ignoring the reversal of direction. 2 N s only removes the downward momentum. 4 N s assumes the ball bounces back with the same speed of 10 m/s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', impulse

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A bomb at rest explodes into two fragments whose masses are in the ratio 1 : 2. Just after the explosion, the ratio of the kinetic energy of the lighter fragment to that of the heavier fragment is:

solution.concept: Momentum conservation in an explosion with K = p²/2m
solution.explanation: The total momentum is zero before the explosion, so the two fragments have momenta equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. With equal p, K = p²/2m is inversely proportional to the mass.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 makes kinetic energy proportional to mass. 1 : 4 and 4 : 1 square the mass ratio, as if the speeds were equal or the momentum ratio were squared incorrectly.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A constant horizontal force of 10 N acts for 3 s on a body of mass 2 kg lying at rest on a smooth horizontal surface, and is then removed. The distance the body covers in the first 5 s from the start is:

solution.concept: Accelerated motion followed by motion with constant velocity (first law)
solution.explanation: While the force acts the body accelerates at F/m. Once the force is removed the net force is zero, so by the first law the body keeps the velocity it has gained.
steps: a = 10/2 = 5 m/s²; distance in 3 s = ½ × 5 × 9 = 22.5 m
Next 2 s at constant velocity: 15 × 2 = 30 m
solution.why_others_wrong: 62.5 m assumes the force acts for all 5 s. 22.5 m assumes the body stops when the force is removed. 37.5 m adds only one second of uniform motion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's first and second laws

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a car speeds up along a level road, the frictional force exerted by the road on its driven wheels is directed forward, in the direction of the car's motion.
Statement II: A box placed on the floor of a truck that is speeding up along a level road, without the box slipping, experiences a static frictional force directed backward, opposite to the truck's motion.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Direction of static friction
solution.explanation: Friction opposes relative motion (or impending relative motion) between surfaces in contact, not the motion of the body. A driven wheel pushes the road backward at the contact point, so the road pushes the car forward. The box tends to slide backward relative to the accelerating floor, so static friction on it acts forward; this is the only horizontal force that can accelerate the box with the truck.
steps: Statement I: forward friction on the driven wheels accelerates the car (true)
Statement II: friction on the box must be forward to give it the truck's acceleration (false)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II assumes friction always acts against the direction of motion; here it is the force that produces the motion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A small stone of mass 0.5 kg is in each of the situations in List-I. Take g = 10 m/s² and neglect air resistance. Match List-I (situation) with List-II (magnitude of the net force on the stone).

List-I:
A. Just after it is released from rest from a window, falling freely
B. Resting on the floor of a lift that moves upward with a constant velocity
C. Resting on the floor of a lift that is accelerating upward at 2 m/s²
D. Moving in a circle of radius 0.5 m at a constant speed of 2 m/s on a smooth horizontal table, held by a string

List-II:
I. 0
II. 1 N
III. 4 N
IV. 5 N

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Net force equals mass times acceleration
solution.explanation: In every case the net force is simply m times the acceleration of the stone, whatever forces make it up.
steps: D: F = mv²/r = 0.5 × 4/0.5 = 4 N, towards the centre (III)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes give the stone at rest in the lift a non-zero net force, or confuse the net force in the accelerating lift (ma) with the normal force m(g + a) = 6 N.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law and circular motion
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text: A circular road of radius 30 m is banked at 45°. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², the minimum speed at which a car can go round the curve without sliding down the slope is:

solution.concept: Banked road: friction acting up the slope at low speed
solution.explanation: Below the speed for which no friction is needed, the car tends to slide down the slope, so friction acts up the slope. At the minimum speed this friction is limiting (μN).
steps: Vertical: N cos θ + μN sin θ = mg
Horizontal: N sin θ − μN cos θ = mv²/r
solution.why_others_wrong: 10√3 m/s is the speed that needs no friction (√(rg tan θ)). 30 m/s is the maximum safe speed, with friction down the slope. 5√6 m/s drops the denominator (1 + μ tan θ).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', circular motion: car on a banked road

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 5 kg rests on a rough plane inclined at 37° to the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). The coefficient of static friction between the block and the plane is 0.5. A force F is applied to the block parallel to the incline, pointing up the slope. Taking g = 10 m/s², the block stays at rest for:

solution.concept: Range of an applied force for which static friction can hold a block
solution.explanation: Static friction can act either way along the incline, up to μₛN. At the lower limit the block is about to slide down (friction up the slope); at the upper limit it is about to slide up (friction down the slope).
steps: N = mg cos θ = 40 N → f_max = 0.5 × 40 = 20 N; mg sin θ = 30 N
About to slide down: F + 20 = 30 → F = 10 N
About to slide up: F = 30 + 20 = 50 N
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 ≤ F ≤ 50 N forgets that tan 37° = 0.75 > 0.5, so without help the block slides down. 10 N ≤ F ≤ 30 N lets friction act only up the slope. F = 30 N only ignores static friction altogether.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction (static friction on an inclined plane)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A block of mass 2 kg is placed on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction between the block and the plane are 0.7 and 0.5. Take g = 10 m/s². Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Left to itself, the block stays at rest on the incline.
(b) While the block is at rest, the total force exerted by the plane on it is 20 N, directed vertically upward.
(c) While the block is at rest, the friction force on it equals μₛ times the normal reaction.
(d) If the block is set sliding down the incline and then left to itself, it keeps speeding up.
(e) The normal reaction on the block is 20 N.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Static and kinetic friction on an incline
solution.explanation: The block stays at rest if tan θ ≤ μₛ. At rest, gravity is balanced by the plane, so the plane's total force (normal force plus friction) is equal and opposite to the weight. Once sliding, kinetic friction μₖN is smaller, and if tan θ > μₖ the block accelerates down.
steps: (c) Friction = mg sin 30° = 10 N, less than μₛN = 0.7 × 17.3 = 12.1 N (false)
(d) tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.5 → net force down the incline = 10 − 8.66 > 0 (true)
(e) N = mg cos 30° = 10√3 ≈ 17.3 N, not 20 N (false)
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) treats static friction as always limiting; (e) forgets the factor cos θ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A shell is fired from level ground with a speed of 20√2 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. At the highest point of its path it explodes into two fragments of equal mass. One fragment falls vertically downward, starting from rest just after the explosion. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the other fragment lands at a distance from the point of firing of:

solution.concept: Conservation of momentum in an explosion during projectile motion
solution.explanation: The explosion forces are internal and act for a very short time, so the horizontal momentum just before and just after the explosion is the same. If one half is left at rest, the other half carries all the momentum and moves horizontally with twice the shell's speed. Both halves take the same time to fall as the shell would have taken to come down.
steps: Range of the shell R = u² sin 90°/g = 800/10 = 80 m; top is at 40 m
Speed at top = 20√2 cos 45° = 20 m/s → other fragment: (m/2)v = m × 20 → v = 40 m/s
Fall time from top = u sin 45°/g = 2 s → extra distance = 40 × 2 = 80 m
solution.shortcut: The second fragment lands at R/2 + R = 1.5R = 120 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 m is where the unbroken shell would land. 160 m doubles the whole range. 200 m lets the fragment move at 40 m/s for the full 4 s time of flight instead of only the 2 s of its fall.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: A constant force F = (3î + 4ĵ) N acts on a particle while it undergoes a displacement d = (2î − ĵ + 5k̂) m. The work done by the force is:

solution.concept: Work as the scalar product of force and displacement
solution.explanation: W = F · d = FₓDₓ + F_yD_y + F_zD_z. Components of the displacement along which the force has no component contribute nothing.
solution.why_others_wrong: −2 J reverses the sign of the result. 10 J ignores the negative sign of the y-component of d. 5√30 J multiplies the magnitudes, as if F and d were parallel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', notions of work and kinetic energy (scalar product)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The speed of a ball of mass 0.5 kg increases from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. The work done by the net force on the ball is:

solution.concept: Work-energy theorem
solution.explanation: The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy, W = ½mv² − ½mu².
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 J uses the square of the change in speed, (6 − 2)², instead of the change in the squares. 9 J is the final kinetic energy alone. 16 J drops the factor ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The extension of an ideal spring, within its elastic limit, is doubled. The elastic potential energy stored in it becomes:

solution.concept: Potential energy of a spring
solution.explanation: The potential energy of a spring stretched by x is ½kx², proportional to the square of the extension.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Twice' treats U as proportional to x (true of the spring force, not of the energy). The others ignore the dependence on x.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring
solution.final_answer: Option B: four times its earlier value

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass 4 kg has a linear momentum of magnitude 20 kg m/s. Its kinetic energy is:

solution.concept: Relation between kinetic energy and momentum
solution.explanation: K = ½mv² and p = mv, so K = p²/2m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 J drops the factor 2 in the denominator. 40 J computes pm/2 instead of p²/2m. 5 J is only the speed p/m = 5 m/s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', kinetic energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electric pump raises 600 kg of water per minute through a height of 10 m. The efficiency of the pump is 80%. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting the kinetic energy given to the water, the electrical power drawn by the pump is:

solution.concept: Power and efficiency
solution.explanation: The useful (output) power is the rate of gain of potential energy of the water. Efficiency is output power divided by input power, so the input is the output divided by 0.8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1000 W is the useful output, not the power drawn. 800 W multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing. 60 kW takes the energy per minute (60 000 J) as the power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: A force F = (6 − 2x) N, where x is in metres, acts along the x-axis on a particle. The work done by this force as the particle moves from x = 0 to x = 4 m is:

solution.concept: Work done by a variable force as an integral
solution.explanation: W = ∫F dx. The force is positive up to x = 3 m and negative beyond it, so the area under the F–x graph between 3 m and 4 m counts as negative work.
steps: (Check: +9 J from 0 to 3 m and −1 J from 3 to 4 m)
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 J stops at x = 3 m, where the force becomes zero. 10 J adds the magnitude of the negative area. 24 J treats the force as constant at its initial value of 6 N.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work done by a variable force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small bob of mass m, tied to a light string, is whirled in a vertical circle with the least speed that lets it just complete the circle. Neglecting air resistance, the tension in the string when the string is horizontal is:

solution.concept: Energy conservation and the radial equation in a vertical circle
solution.explanation: Just completing the circle means the tension is zero at the top, so v_top² = gr. Coming down to the level of the centre, the bob falls through r. With the string horizontal, gravity is perpendicular to it, so the tension alone provides the centripetal force.
solution.why_others_wrong: mg is the tension when the bob hangs at rest. 2mg uses v² = 2gr, forgetting the speed at the top. 6mg is the tension at the lowest point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', motion in a vertical circle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s on a smooth horizontal surface collides head-on with a block of mass 1 kg moving towards it at 3 m/s. The two blocks stick together. The loss of kinetic energy in the collision is:

solution.concept: Perfectly inelastic collision: momentum conserved, kinetic energy lost
solution.explanation: Momentum is conserved (with signs for the opposite directions), giving the common velocity. The loss is the initial total kinetic energy minus the final one.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13.5 J assumes the blocks stop dead. 1.5 J is the kinetic energy left after the collision. 6 J halves the loss.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions (completely inelastic collision)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The work needed to push a box slowly up a smooth inclined plane to a height h is the same as the work needed to lift it slowly and vertically through the same height h.
Statement II: Pushing the box slowly up the smooth inclined plane needs a smaller force than lifting it slowly and vertically.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Work against gravity is path independent
solution.explanation: Moving the box slowly means its kinetic energy does not change, so the work done by the applied force equals the gain in potential energy, mgh, whatever the path. On the smooth incline the force needed is only mg sin θ, smaller than mg, but it acts over a longer distance h/sin θ, so the product is still mgh.
steps: Incline: F = mg sin θ, distance = h/sin θ → W = mgh
Vertical: F = mg, distance = h → W = mgh
mg sin θ < mg → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true: the incline trades a smaller force for a longer distance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy (conservative force)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car of mass 500 kg starts from rest on a level road. Its engine delivers a constant power of 10 kW to it. Neglecting friction and air resistance, the speed of the car after 10 s is:

solution.concept: Constant power: energy, not force, grows uniformly
solution.explanation: With constant power the force P/v falls as the car speeds up, so the acceleration is not uniform. The energy delivered, however, is P t, and all of it becomes kinetic energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10√2 m/s writes the kinetic energy as mv² instead of ½mv². 200 m/s equates Pt to the momentum mv. About 0.63 m/s takes the power as 10 W instead of 10 kW.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power and the work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 1 kg slides at 3 m/s on a rough horizontal floor (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.25) and hits the free end of a light horizontal spring of spring constant 200 N/m, whose other end is fixed to a wall. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum compression of the spring is:

solution.concept: Work-energy theorem with a spring and friction
solution.explanation: During compression the block's kinetic energy goes partly into the spring's potential energy and partly into work against friction over the compression x.
solution.why_others_wrong: About 21.2 cm ignores friction. 22.5 cm adds the friction term with the wrong sign, as if friction helped compress the spring. About 14 cm writes the spring energy as kx² instead of ½kx².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small ball is released from rest on a smooth track that runs down into a vertical circular loop of radius 0.4 m, the ball moving on the inside of the loop. The minimum height above the bottom of the loop from which it must be released to go round the loop without losing contact with the track is:

solution.concept: Condition for looping the loop, with energy conservation
solution.explanation: At the top of the loop the normal force may at most fall to zero, so gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: v_top² ≥ gR. Energy conservation from the release point then gives the least release height.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.8 m (2R) only reaches the top with zero speed, so the ball falls off before it gets there. 1.2 m (3R) and 2.0 m (5R) are larger than needed; 5R comes from confusing v² = 5gR at the bottom with a height.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', motion in a vertical circle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A block of mass 2 kg is pulled at a constant speed through 5 m up a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal, by a force parallel to the plane. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 1/(2√3). Take g = 10 m/s². Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The work done by the applied force is 75 J.
(b) The work done by gravity on the block is −50 J.
(c) The work done by friction on the block is −50 J.
(d) The work done by the normal reaction on the block is zero.
(e) The total work done by all the forces on the block is 75 J.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Work done by individual forces and the work-energy theorem
solution.explanation: At constant speed the change in kinetic energy is zero, so the total work by all forces is zero. The applied force balances gravity's component along the incline plus kinetic friction.
steps: Height gained = 5 sin 30° = 2.5 m → W_gravity = −20 × 2.5 = −50 J (b true)
Friction = μmg cos 30° = (1/(2√3)) × 20 × (√3/2) = 5 N → W_friction = −25 J (c false)
Applied force = 10 + 5 = 15 N → W = 75 J (a true)
Normal force ⟂ displacement → zero work (d true)
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) takes friction equal to the gravity component; (e) forgets that constant speed means zero total work.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform circular disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates at 10 rad/s about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane. The magnitude of its angular momentum about this axis is:

solution.concept: Angular momentum of a rigid body about a fixed axis
solution.explanation: For rotation about a fixed axis, L = Iω. For a uniform disc about its own axis, I = ½MR².
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 uses MR² (a ring). 1.25 uses ¼MR², the disc's moment of inertia about a diameter. 10 multiplies M, R and ω, mixing up L with the momentum of a point mass at the rim.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular momentum in case of rotation about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A crowbar of length 1.0 m rests on a fulcrum 0.2 m from the end that is under a load of 400 N. Neglecting the weight of the crowbar, the least force that must be applied perpendicular to the bar at its other end to lift the load is:

solution.concept: Principle of moments (lever)
solution.explanation: For a lever in equilibrium, the moments about the fulcrum balance: load × load arm = effort × effort arm. Here the load arm is 0.2 m and the effort arm is 1.0 − 0.2 = 0.8 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1600 N inverts the ratio of the arms. 400 N ignores the lever action. 80 N takes the whole length of the bar (1.0 m) as the effort arm.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', principle of moments

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wheel of radius 0.3 m rotates about its fixed axle at 120 revolutions per minute. The linear speed of a point on its rim is:

solution.concept: Relation between linear and angular speed, v = ωr
solution.explanation: Convert the rate of rotation to rad/s first: 1 revolution = 2π rad. Every point of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis has the same ω, and v = ωr for a point at distance r from the axis.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.6 m/s uses 2 rev/s as if it were 2 rad/s. 36 m/s multiplies 120 rev/min by r without any conversion. 2.4π m/s uses the diameter instead of the radius.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular velocity and its relation with linear velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A thin uniform ring has a larger moment of inertia than a uniform disc of the same mass and radius, both about the axis through the centre perpendicular to the plane.
Reason (R): In the ring, all of the mass lies at the greatest distance R from this axis, while in the disc much of the mass lies closer to the axis.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Moment of inertia depends on the distribution of mass about the axis
solution.explanation: I = Σmr². Moving mass farther from the axis raises I. The ring has I = MR², the disc only ½MR², because the disc's mass is spread from r = 0 to r = R.
steps: Ring: every element at r = R → I = MR²
Disc: elements from 0 to R → I = ½MR²
R states exactly why the ring's I is larger → A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, and R is the reason for A, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two particles of masses 1 kg and 3 kg are initially at rest, 8 m apart, in free space. They move towards each other only because of their mutual gravitational attraction. When they collide, the distance moved by the 1 kg particle is:

solution.concept: Centre of mass stays at rest when only internal forces act
solution.explanation: The mutual attraction is an internal force of the two-particle system, and no external force acts. The centre of mass, at rest initially, stays at rest, so the particles meet there.
steps: Place 1 kg at x = 0 and 3 kg at x = 8 m
The 1 kg particle moves 6 m (the 3 kg one moves 2 m)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 m is the distance moved by the 3 kg particle. 4 m assumes they meet at the midpoint, as for equal masses. 8 m assumes the heavier particle stays fixed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', motion of centre of mass

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: Four small balls, each of mass 0.5 kg, are fixed at the corners of a light square frame of side 0.2 m. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis along one diagonal of the square is:

solution.concept: Moment of inertia of a system of point masses
solution.explanation: I = Σmr², where r is each ball's perpendicular distance from the axis. The two balls on the diagonal lie on the axis (r = 0); the other two are at half the length of the other diagonal, a/√2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.04 kg m² is the moment of inertia about a side (or about the perpendicular axis through the centre). 0.08 kg m² is about the perpendicular axis through a corner. 0.01 kg m² counts only one ball.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: Two uniform circular discs have the same mass and the same thickness. One is made of iron and the other of aluminium (aluminium is less dense than iron). About the axis through the centre perpendicular to the plane:

options.text: the iron disc has the larger moment of inertia
both discs have the same moment of inertia, since their masses are equal
the aluminium disc has the larger moment of inertia
the ratio of their moments of inertia equals the ratio of their densities

solution.concept: Moment of inertia depends on size, not only on mass
solution.explanation: Same mass and thickness means the less dense aluminium disc must have a larger area, i.e. a larger radius. Since I = ½MR² for each disc, the larger radius gives the larger moment of inertia.
steps: M = ρ(πR²)t, with M and t equal → R² ∝ 1/ρ
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options ignore that, for equal mass, the less dense material forms a wider disc with its mass farther from the axis. In fact I ∝ R² ∝ 1/ρ, so the ratio of the moments of inertia is the inverse ratio of the densities.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia
solution.final_answer: Option C: the aluminium disc has the larger moment of inertia

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A rigid body, initially at rest in free space, is acted on only by the forces described in List-I. Match List-I (forces) with List-II (resulting motion).

List-I:
A. Two equal and opposite forces acting along the same line
B. Two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action are different (a couple)
C. A single force whose line of action passes through the centre of mass
D. A single force whose line of action does not pass through the centre of mass

List-II:
I. Both translation and rotation
II. Rotation without translation
III. Translation without rotation
IV. Neither translation nor rotation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Translational and rotational equilibrium
solution.explanation: Translation is decided by the net force, rotation by the net torque. Two equal and opposite forces give zero net force; their torque is zero only if they share a line of action. A single force always gives a net force; it gives a torque about the centre of mass only if its line misses the centre of mass.
steps: C: ΣF ≠ 0, Στ about CM = 0 → III
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the effects of a couple and of a single force through the centre of mass, or of the two cases of a single force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', equilibrium of a rigid body and couple
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A wheel whose moment of inertia about its fixed axle is 0.5 kg m² starts from rest. A constant torque of 2 N m acts on it about the axle for 5 s. Neglecting friction, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its angular acceleration is 4 rad/s².
(b) Its angular velocity at the end of 5 s is 20 rad/s.
(c) It turns through 100 rad in the 5 s.
(d) Its rotational kinetic energy at the end of 5 s is 100 J.
(e) Its angular momentum about the axle at the end of 5 s is 10 kg m² s⁻¹.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rotation with constant angular acceleration
solution.explanation: τ = Iα gives a constant α, after which the equations of rotational kinematics apply exactly as their linear counterparts do.
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) drops the ½ in θ = ½αt²; every option that includes (c) or leaves out (a) is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', kinematics and dynamics of rotational motion about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Blocks of masses 3 kg and 1 kg hang at the two ends of a light string that passes over a pulley in the form of a uniform disc of mass 4 kg, which rotates without friction about a fixed horizontal axle through its centre. The string does not slip on the pulley. Taking g = 10 m/s², the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks is:

solution.concept: Coupled translation and rotation (pulley with moment of inertia)
solution.explanation: Because the pulley has a moment of inertia, the tensions on the two sides differ. Their difference supplies the torque Iα, with a = αr since the string does not slip.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 m/s² treats the pulley as massless. 2.5 m/s² takes the pulley's moment of inertia as Mr² (a ring). 10 m/s² leaves out the masses of the blocks from the inertia.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', dynamics of rotational motion about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two discs rotate about the same fixed axle without friction. Disc P (moment of inertia 2 kg m²) spins at 10 rad/s, and disc Q (moment of inertia 3 kg m²) spins at 5 rad/s in the opposite sense. They are brought into contact along the axle and soon rotate together. The kinetic energy lost in the process is:

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum with opposite senses of rotation
solution.explanation: Only internal torques (friction between the discs) act, so the total angular momentum about the axle is conserved. Angular momenta in opposite senses must be given opposite signs.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 J treats both discs as spinning in the same sense (common ω = 7 rad/s). 137.5 J assumes the discs stop. 2.5 J is the kinetic energy left, not the energy lost.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A uniform rod, hinged at one end so that it can turn freely in a vertical plane, is held horizontal and released. Just after release, the upward force exerted by the hinge on the rod is less than the weight of the rod.
Reason (R): Just after release, the centre of mass of the rod has a downward acceleration.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Hinge reaction on a rotating rod
solution.explanation: Just after release the rod has no angular velocity, so the only acceleration of its centre of mass is the tangential one, downward. Newton's second law for the centre of mass, Mg − N = Ma_cm, then makes N less than Mg. With α = 3g/2L from τ = Iα (I = ML²/3), a_cm = 3g/4 and N = Mg/4.
steps: Mg − N = M(3g/4) → N = Mg/4 < Mg
solution.why_others_wrong: R is exactly the reason the hinge force falls below the weight, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', motion of centre of mass and dynamics of rotational motion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform horizontal beam of length 6 m and mass 50 kg is hinged at one end to a wall. It is held horizontal by a vertical rope tied to the beam 2 m from the hinge, and a load of mass 25 kg hangs from the free end of the beam. Taking g = 10 m/s², the vertical force exerted by the hinge on the beam is:

solution.concept: Conditions of equilibrium: forces and moments
solution.explanation: Take moments about the hinge to find the rope tension (the hinge force then has no moment). The vertical forces must then add to zero. Because the rope is attached inside the length of the beam, it must pull up with more than the total weight, and the hinge must pull the beam down.
steps: Moments about the hinge: T × 2 = 500 × 3 + 250 × 6 = 3000 → T = 1500 N
The hinge pulls the beam down with 750 N
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Upward' assumes the hinge must support the beam. 1500 N upward is the rope tension. 250 N downward forgets the load's moment when finding the tension.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', equilibrium of a rigid body

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², the magnitude of the gravitational field intensity at a distance of 2 m from a point mass of 10 kg is about:

solution.concept: Gravitational field of a point mass
solution.explanation: The gravitational field intensity is the force per unit mass on a test mass: E = GM/r².
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ divides by r instead of r². 6.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ leaves out the distance. 1.67 × 10⁻¹¹ slips a power of ten.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', universal law of gravitation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two satellites revolve round the Earth in circular orbits of radii r and 4r. The ratio of the orbital speed of the inner satellite to that of the outer satellite is:

solution.concept: Orbital speed and orbital radius
solution.explanation: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). The orbital speed falls as the square root of the radius grows.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 inverts the ratio. 4 : 1 takes v ∝ 1/r. 1 : 4 takes v ∝ r.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', earth satellites

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Treat the Earth as a uniform sphere of radius 6400 km with g = 10 m/s² at its surface, and take the gravitational potential to be zero at infinity. The gravitational potential at the Earth's surface is:

solution.concept: Gravitational potential at the surface in terms of g
solution.explanation: V = −GM/R, and since g = GM/R², GM/R = gR. So V = −gR at the surface.
solution.why_others_wrong: The positive value ignores that gravitational potential is negative (taken zero at infinity). −6.4 × 10⁴ uses R in km. −3.2 × 10⁷ brings in a spurious factor ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Inside a uniform thin spherical shell, the gravitational potential due to the shell is the same at every point and equals its value at the surface of the shell.
Statement II: At the centre of a uniform solid sphere, the gravitational field and the gravitational potential due to the sphere are both zero (potential taken as zero at infinity).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Field and potential inside spherical mass distributions
solution.explanation: Inside a uniform shell the gravitational force (field) is zero, so no work is done in moving a test mass around inside it: the potential is constant and equal to its surface value, −GM/R. At the centre of a solid sphere the field is zero by symmetry, but the potential is not zero: work must be done to take a mass from the centre out to infinity, so the potential there is negative (indeed lower than at the surface).
steps: Shell: E = 0 inside → V constant = −GM/R (Statement I true)
Solid sphere: E = 0 at centre, but V(centre) < V(surface) < 0 (Statement II false)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II wrongly concludes zero potential from zero field; a zero field only means the potential has no slope there.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy and the shell theorem
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: If the radius of the Earth were to shrink by 1% while its mass stayed the same, the acceleration due to gravity at its surface would:

solution.concept: Dependence of g on the radius for a fixed mass
solution.explanation: g = GM/R². With M fixed, g ∝ R⁻², so for a small change Δg/g = −2ΔR/R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Decrease' gets the sign wrong: a smaller radius brings the surface closer to the centre. 1% ignores the square. 'Unchanged' would hold only if g depended on mass alone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity of the earth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A satellite in a circular orbit round the Earth has kinetic energy K. The least additional energy that must be given to it to make it escape from the Earth's gravity is K.
Reason (R): The total mechanical energy of a satellite in a circular orbit is −K, where K is its kinetic energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Energy of an orbiting satellite and the energy to escape
solution.explanation: For a circular orbit, K = GMm/2r and U = −GMm/r, so the total energy is −GMm/2r = −K. To escape, the total energy must be raised to at least zero, so at least K must be added.
steps: Energy to reach E = 0: ΔE = K
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the satellite's total energy, which is exactly what fixes the escape energy in A, so B is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', energy of an orbiting satellite
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three point masses, each of 1 kg, are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 1 m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², the minimum work needed to separate them to infinite distances from one another is about:

solution.concept: Potential energy of a system of particles
solution.explanation: The potential energy of a system of point masses is the sum over every distinct pair of −Gmᵢmⱼ/rᵢⱼ. Three masses form three pairs. The work needed to pull them apart slowly equals −U.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ J counts one pair. 1.33 × 10⁻¹⁰ J counts two pairs. 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ J counts each pair twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A satellite revolves round a planet in a circular orbit just above the planet's surface, with period T. Treating the planet as a uniform sphere and G as the universal gravitational constant, the mean density of the planet is:

solution.concept: Density of a planet from the period of a close satellite
solution.explanation: For an orbit of radius R (just above the surface), T² = 4π²R³/(GM). Writing M = ρ(4/3)πR³ makes R cancel, so the period of a close satellite depends only on the planet's density.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4π²/(GT²) forgets the volume factor (4/3)π. 3/(4πGT²) mishandles π. GT²/(3π) inverts the result and does not even have the dimensions of density.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', earth satellites (period of a satellite)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The escape speed from the Earth's surface is 11.2 km/s. A planet has twice the radius of the Earth and half its mean density. The escape speed from the surface of this planet is about:

solution.concept: Escape speed in terms of radius and density
solution.explanation: vₑ = √(2GM/R) with M = ρ(4/3)πR³ gives vₑ = R√(8πGρ/3), so vₑ ∝ R√ρ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.2 km/s notices that g = (4/3)πGρR is unchanged but forgets that vₑ = √(2gR) also grows with R. 22.4 km/s ignores the change of density. 7.9 km/s divides by √2 instead of multiplying.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', escape speed

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A satellite of mass 100 kg is to be placed in a circular orbit at a height above the Earth's surface equal to the Earth's radius R = 6400 km. Taking g = 10 m/s² at the surface and neglecting the Earth's rotation and air resistance, the minimum energy that must be supplied to it, starting from rest on the surface, is:

solution.concept: Energy to put a satellite into orbit
solution.explanation: The energy supplied equals the satellite's total energy in orbit minus its energy at rest on the surface. In an orbit of radius r = 2R, E = −GMm/(2r) = −GMm/(4R); on the surface (at rest), E = −GMm/R. Use GM = gR².
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.2 × 10⁹ J is only the gain in potential energy (mgR/2), with no kinetic energy for orbiting. 6.4 × 10⁹ J is mgR, the energy to escape from rest. 1.6 × 10⁹ J is only the kinetic energy in orbit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', energy of an orbiting satellite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: If water (density 1000 kg/m³) were used instead of mercury in a simple barometer, the height of the water column supported by an atmospheric pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa would be (g = 10 m/s²):

solution.concept: Pressure of a liquid column
solution.explanation: The atmosphere supports a liquid column whose pressure hρg equals the atmospheric pressure. A less dense liquid needs a taller column.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.76 m is the height of a mercury barometer. 1 m and 100 m are slips by a factor of 10 in ρg.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', atmospheric pressure and gauge pressure

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin uniform metal plate has a circular hole cut in it. When the plate is heated uniformly, the diameter of the hole:

options.text: increases or decreases depending on the size of the hole

solution.concept: Thermal expansion of a plate with a hole
solution.explanation: On uniform heating every linear dimension of the plate grows by the same fraction αΔT, just as in a photographic enlargement. The hole expands exactly as a disc of the same metal filling it would.
steps: The hole's diameter is such a length → it increases
solution.why_others_wrong: The metal does not expand 'into' the hole; every distance between points of the plate, including across the hole, grows by the same fraction, whatever the hole's size.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A temperature of 50 °C, expressed on the Fahrenheit scale, is:

solution.concept: Relation between the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales
solution.explanation: The ice and steam points are 0 °C and 32 °F, and 100 °C and 212 °F. So t_F − 32 = (180/100) t_C, i.e. t_F = (9/5)t_C + 32.
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 °F forgets to add 32. 82 °F only adds 32. 59.8 °F uses the factor 5/9 instead of 9/5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', temperature and heat (measurement of temperature)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The spectrum of the Sun's radiation has its maximum intensity at a wavelength of about 480 nm. Treating the Sun as a black body and taking Wien's constant as 2.88 × 10⁻³ m K, the temperature of its surface is about:

solution.concept: Wien's displacement law
solution.explanation: Wien's law states λₘT = b: the wavelength of maximum emission times the absolute temperature is a constant.
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 K and 60 000 K slip the power of ten in 480 nm = 4.8 × 10⁻⁷ m. 1.4 × 10⁻⁹ K multiplies b by λₘ instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', blackbody radiation (Wien's displacement law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A metal lid that is stuck tight on a glass jar can often be loosened by pouring hot water over the lid.
Reason (R): For the same rise in temperature, the metal of the lid expands more than the glass of the jar, because its coefficient of thermal expansion is larger.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Differential thermal expansion
solution.explanation: Heating the lid makes it expand. Since the metal's coefficient of expansion is larger than that of glass, the lid grows more than the neck of the jar and the grip loosens.
steps: α_metal > α_glass → the lid's diameter grows more than the neck's → A, explained by R
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R is the reason the lid loosens, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A solid metal sphere of bulk modulus 1.0 × 10¹¹ N/m² is lowered from the surface of the sea to a depth of 1000 m. Taking the density of sea water as 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s², the fractional decrease in its volume is:

solution.concept: Hydraulic stress and bulk modulus
solution.explanation: The extra pressure at a depth h is hρg (the atmospheric pressure acts at the surface as well, so it cancels in the change). Bulk modulus B = Δp/(ΔV/V), so ΔV/V = Δp/B.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1%, 1% and 0.001% are slips by powers of ten in Δp or in converting 10⁻⁴ into a percentage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', bulk modulus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A large closed tank contains water (density 1000 kg/m³). The air above the water is at a pressure 3.0 × 10⁴ Pa above atmospheric pressure. Water flows out into the atmosphere through a small hole in the side of the tank, 2.0 m below the water surface. Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed of efflux is:

solution.concept: Bernoulli's principle for efflux from a pressurised tank
solution.explanation: Apply Bernoulli's equation between the water surface (speed ≈ 0 in a large tank, pressure P₀ + p) and the jet at the hole (pressure P₀). Both the excess pressure and the depth drive the flow.
solution.why_others_wrong: About 6.3 m/s uses Torricelli's √(2gh) and ignores the excess air pressure. About 7.7 m/s ignores the depth. About 8.4 m/s forgets to double the pressure term.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Bernoulli's principle (speed of efflux)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small air bubble of radius 1.5 mm rises slowly through a liquid of density 1000 kg/m³ and coefficient of viscosity 0.5 Pa s. Neglecting the density of air, taking g = 10 m/s² and assuming Stokes' law holds, its terminal velocity is:

solution.concept: Terminal velocity when the body is lighter than the fluid
solution.explanation: The terminal velocity is v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), where ρ is the density of the body and σ that of the fluid. For a bubble ρ ≈ 0, so v is negative: the bubble moves upward, with buoyancy balanced by weight (negligible) plus the downward viscous drag.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Downward' ignores that the bubble is lighter than the liquid. 4.5 cm/s leaves out the factor 2/9. 0.5 cm/s uses 1/9 instead of 2/9.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Stokes' law (terminal velocity)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin horizontal wire ring of radius 2 cm rests on the surface of water (surface tension 0.07 N/m, angle of contact 0°). Neglecting the weight of the ring, the extra force needed to pull it vertically off the surface is about:

solution.concept: Force of surface tension on a ring with two contact lines
solution.explanation: As the ring is lifted, a film of water clings to it along both its inner and its outer edge. Surface tension pulls down along each edge, so the total length in contact is twice the circumference.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.8π × 10⁻³ N counts only one edge. 1.4π × 10⁻³ N uses πr instead of 2πr for one edge. 11.2π × 10⁻³ N counts each edge twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface tension

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (thermal quantity) with List-II (its SI unit).

List-I:
A. Specific heat capacity
B. Molar specific heat capacity
C. Latent heat
D. Heat capacity of a body

List-II:
I. J kg⁻¹
II. J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
III. J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
IV. J K⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Definitions of heat capacity, specific heat and latent heat
solution.explanation: Heat capacity S = ΔQ/ΔT belongs to a whole body. Dividing by its mass gives the specific heat capacity, and dividing by the amount of substance gives the molar specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the heat per unit mass for a change of state, which happens without a change in temperature, so it has no K⁻¹.
steps: Specific heat: ΔQ/(mΔT) → J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (II)
Molar specific heat: ΔQ/(μΔT) → J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (III)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes give latent heat a K⁻¹ (it involves no temperature change) or swap the heat capacity of a body with the specific heat capacity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', specific heat capacity and latent heat
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When heat is conducted through a rod in the steady state, the temperature at each point of the rod does not change with time.
Statement II: In the steady state of conduction through a uniform rod with insulated sides, the temperature falls uniformly (linearly) with distance along the rod, from the hot end to the cold end.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Steady-state conduction
solution.explanation: In the steady state no part of the rod is still absorbing heat, so every temperature stays fixed. With insulated sides, the same heat current H = KA(dT/dx) passes every cross-section; for a uniform rod K and A are constant, so the temperature gradient is the same everywhere.
steps: Steady state → temperatures constant in time (I true)
H, K and A constant along the rod → dT/dx constant → linear fall (II true)
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true for a uniform rod with insulated sides, so options B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', heat transfer (conduction)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform steel wire 10 m long hangs vertically from a rigid support with nothing attached to its lower end. The density of steel is 8000 kg/m³ and its Young's modulus is 2 × 10¹¹ N/m². Taking g = 10 m/s², the extension of the wire due to its own weight is:

solution.concept: Extension of a wire under its own weight
solution.explanation: The tension is not uniform: at a distance x above the lower end it equals the weight of the wire below, ρAgx. Each element dx stretches by (ρAgx/AY)dx, and adding these up gives half of what the whole weight would produce if it hung at the bottom.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.04 mm treats the whole weight as acting at the lower end (uniform tension). 0.01 mm halves twice. 2 mm is a slip by a factor of 100.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Young's modulus

questions.subject: Physics
